lesson.title: Setting the Bar: How to Choose a Significance Level
lesson.summary: Choosing alpha means deciding, before any data are collected, how much risk of a false alarm you are willing to accept, and that decision should be driven by the real-world cost of each kind of mistake, not by habit.
lesson.body:
Alpha directly sets the Type I error rate, as established in the last two chapters. Because Type I and Type II error trade off against each other for a fixed sample size, a point developed fully in the next chapter, choosing alpha is really choosing how to balance the risk of a false alarm against the risk of a missed detection. There is no universally correct alpha, the right choice depends on which mistake is worse in the specific situation at hand.

A few real settings make this concrete. Criminal trials effectively use a very strict standard, "beyond a reasonable doubt," because convicting an innocent person, a Type I error if H0 represents innocence, is considered far worse than letting a guilty person go free. Approving a drug for a serious, otherwise untreatable disease might justify tolerating a somewhat larger alpha than usual, because missing a genuinely effective treatment, a Type II error, could cost lives, while a mistaken approval can still face further review down the line. Routine manufacturing quality control might comfortably use alpha = 0.05 or even 0.10, since flagging a machine for inspection, a possible Type I error, is cheap compared to shipping an entire batch of defective product, a Type II error.

Return once more to the cereal boxes, where p = 0.0456. If the quality control department had pre-committed to alpha = 0.05, a fairly typical choice when investigating a machine is low cost, this result triggers a rejection of H0 and a recalibration check. If instead the department had pre-committed to alpha = 0.01, perhaps because recalibrating the production line is expensive and disruptive and they want to be quite sure before shutting it down, that same p = 0.0456 would not trigger a rejection, and the machine would be left running. Neither choice is wrong in a vacuum, they simply encode different judgments about which mistake, an unnecessary shutdown versus continuing to underfill boxes, is costlier to the company.

The practical guidance is straightforward: choose alpha before collecting data, choose it based on the real consequences of Type I versus Type II errors in context, and report it honestly no matter how the data turn out. Never adjust alpha after seeing the p-value just to reach a preferred conclusion, that is the same kind of after-the-fact manipulation warned about when choosing between one-sided and two-sided tests.
